title: Lake Powell WY2026 operations are persistently framed around critical-elevation protection and unprecedented drought response.
summary: Across all four TR-A sources (official USBR operations page, 24-Month Study, 2026 DROA Plan, CRSP Fact Sheet) and the TR-C media sources, the dominant operational frame is not normal tier-based release management but emergency protection of elevations above 3,500 ft. Every authoritative source in this corpus is anchored to the drought response vocabulary: DROA activation, release reductions to legal minimum, Flaming Gorge draws, and minimum power pool protection.
interpretation: This is a stable cross-document pattern, not a coincidence of source selection. All four official sources were independently produced but converge on the same drought-response narrative. This is stronger evidence than any single source that WY2026 represents a genuine operational emergency, not a routine tier adjustment.

title: Three specific elevation thresholds (3,525 ft, 3,490 ft, 3,500 ft) appear independently across authoritative and infrastructure sources and together define the operational ladder.
summary: Three elevation thresholds are independently stated in multiple sources: the DROA Target Elevation of 3,525 ft appears in LP-DEMO-A-003, LP-DEMO-A-004, and is implied in LP-DEMO-A-001/A-002 (release reductions made because Powell was projected below it). The minimum power pool of 3,490 ft appears in LP-DEMO-A-003, LP-DEMO-A-004, and LP-DEMO-C-002. The operational redline of 3,500 ft appears in LP-DEMO-C-002. Together, these three thresholds define a four-state operational ladder: above 3,525 ft (standard DROA operations), 3,525–3,500 ft (DROA response window), 3,500–3,490 ft (engineering risk zone, hydropower protected), below 3,490 ft (penstock failure, outlet works only).
interpretation: The independent appearance of these thresholds in both official rule documents (A-003, A-004) and engineering-analysis sources (C-002) cross-validates them as genuine operational anchors, not source-specific estimates. The four-state ladder is not stated as such in any single document — it emerges only through synthesis.

title: The 24-Month Study, DROA activation, and Section 6.E emergency authority form one integrated decision chain — each activating the next.
summary: KUs from LP-DEMO-A-001, LP-DEMO-A-002, and LP-DEMO-A-003 together reveal a sequential decision chain: (1) August 2025 24-Month Study sets the WY2026 tier at Mid-Elevation Release; (2) subsequent study iterations project Lake Powell dropping below 3,525 ft, triggering DROA; (3) DROA requires GCD monthly adjustments first; (4) conditions further deteriorate, activating Section 6.E DOI authority to reduce annual release from 7.48 to 6.0 maf; (5) May 2026 24-Month Study formally incorporates 1.0 MAF DROA Flaming Gorge release as a model input. No single source captures this full chain — each documents its own step.
interpretation: The five-step decision chain is a synthesis finding, not an observation from any single source. The complementary nature of these sources is the key discovery: they each capture one decision stage and together reveal the full escalation logic.

title: Research on forecast horizons (B-002) provides external validation for why the 24-Month Study's snowpack-based inflow forecasting is central to Lake Powell release decisions.
summary: KU-LP-DEMO-013 (from research paper LP-DEMO-B-002) establishes that approximately 80% of large US reservoirs use medium-to-long range inflow forecasts and that western high-elevation systems use snowpack-based long-range horizons. This independently validates the 24-Month Study's reliance on CBRFC snowpack-based inflow forecasting as the primary input to Lake Powell release decisions — not as a system-specific design choice, but as the standard operational approach for reservoirs of this type. Combined with KU-LP-DEMO-014's finding that forecast-informed models outperform models neglecting the horizon, the research corpus provides an external basis for evaluating whether CRSS modeling of Lake Powell operations is methodologically aligned with best practice.
interpretation: The TR-B research source provides an external reference point that the TR-A official sources cannot: it shows that the 24-Month Study's forecasting approach is standard, but also raises the question of whether the underlying CRSS model handles the forecast horizon correctly. This is a useful methodological anchor for the research relevance layer.

title: The 7.48 maf and 6.0 maf WY2026 release volumes are a decision-stage sequence, not a factual contradiction.
summary: KU-LP-DEMO-001 documents the 7.48 maf release as the standard Mid-Elevation Tier baseline established at the August 2025 tier-setting. KU-LP-DEMO-002 documents the 6.0 maf reduction as a subsequent emergency override under Section 6.E. Both values appear in LP-DEMO-A-001 and are also referenced in LP-DEMO-A-002. A reader or retrieval system could interpret the two values as conflicting records about the same operational decision; in fact, they represent two stages of the same decision chain.
interpretation: The discrepancy is procedural, not factual. Treating 7.48 maf and 6.0 maf as contradictions would be an error; they are complementary in that the 7.48 maf value establishes the precedent that makes the 6.0 maf reduction visible as an emergency departure. The knowledge base must preserve both values with decision-stage metadata to prevent misinterpretation.

title: Cutting Lake Powell releases protects reservoir elevation but conflicts with downstream compact delivery obligations and WAPA Basin Fund revenue requirements.
summary: KU-LP-DEMO-002 shows releases were cut to 6.0 maf (unprecedented minimum). KU-LP-DEMO-010 shows that DROA itself requires minimizing impacts to the Basin Fund (75% of which is Glen Canyon hydropower). KU-LP-DEMO-016 shows the 3,500 ft operational redline strands 4.4 MAF below it. And the CRSP system's compact obligation requires delivering specified volumes to the lower basin (CRSP Act, Law of the River). These three constraints — protect elevation, maintain Basin Fund, meet compact delivery — are simultaneously in tension during WY2026, creating a multi-objective optimization problem under extreme hydrology.
interpretation: This tradeoff is the operational core of the WY2026 case study. No single document states all three constraints together; the synthesis layer makes the tension visible for the first time by crossing KUs from official operations (A-001), DROA framework (A-003), CRSP facts (A-004), and infrastructure analysis (C-002).

title: Upstream DROA releases from Flaming Gorge protect Lake Powell in the short term but transfer drought risk to upstream reservoirs, with a finite number of deployments available.
summary: KU-LP-DEMO-008 documents the 2026 DROA Plan calls for 660,000 AF–1 MAF from Flaming Gorge, with no anticipated recovery through the plan year. KU-LP-DEMO-018 reports that Flaming Gorge is projected to lose 35 ft of elevation from the 2026 draws, and that experts characterize this reservoir-triage approach as only usable 'once or twice' before upstream buffers are exhausted. The DROA accounting system (credit/debit) in KU-LP-DEMO-009 assumes water will eventually be restored to Flaming Gorge — but no recovery is anticipated in 2026.
interpretation: The DROA mechanism shifts drought risk upstream on a temporary basis that assumes future hydrologic recovery for replenishment. In WY2026, the 'no anticipated recovery' clause makes this a permanent drain on Flaming Gorge's buffer. Two or three years of similar draws would exhaust Flaming Gorge's DROA-available storage entirely — a cascading vulnerability not visible from any single source document.

title: The source corpus lacks Lake Mead coordination data, Post-2026 rule development documents, and LP-DEMO-B-001 modeling content.
summary: Three substantive evidence gaps in this 8-source corpus limit synthesis scope: (1) Lake Mead coordination — KU-LP-DEMO-018 mentions Lake Mead 'approaching its own shortage thresholds' but no LP-DEMO source provides Lake Mead elevation data, Tier 2 shortage conditions, or Lower Basin compact delivery impacts. (2) Post-2026 rule development — the WY2026 crisis makes the expiration of the 2007 Interim Guidelines especially consequential, but no source in this corpus addresses the Post-2026 EIS or LROC criteria. (3) LP-DEMO-B-001 (Modeling Impacts of Glen Canyon Dam Operations on Colorado River Resources) — the PDF download returned only 77 chars of content (paywall/redirect), leaving the modeling/ecology linkage entirely unaddressed.

Addressing them would require acquiring: the June 2026 Lake Mead 24-Month Study outputs, the Post-2026 Draft EIS public comment document, and a paywall-accessible copy of LP-DEMO-B-001. Each gap limits the ability to make cross-system synthesis claims about the full Colorado River Basin.

title: Glen Canyon Dam infrastructure cannot reliably operate below 3,500 ft; engineering modifications are 2+ years away, leaving current DROA measures as the only available buffer.
summary: KU-LP-DEMO-015, 016, and 017 together establish that: (1) the river outlet works are not rated for sustained use below 3,490 ft, suffered cavitation damage in 2023, and are functionally limited at 3,394 ft; (2) Reclamation's practical redline of 3,500 ft strands 4.4 MAF below it; (3) three engineering modifications are under appraisal study (late 2026/early 2027 expected), but any action requires congressional authorization and multi-year construction. This means there is no infrastructure fix available before WY2027–2028 at the earliest, and the DROA-based operational response must bridge that gap entirely.
interpretation: This is the central unresolved operational issue for Lake Powell in the 2026–2028 window. The problem is not an operating rule gap or a governance question — it is a physical infrastructure limitation with a known timeline for resolution. The knowledge base should track: appraisal study publication, congressional appropriation, and construction timeline milestones. The engineering gap makes WY2027 a particularly vulnerable year if hydrology does not recover.
